clue.text: Artist's somewhat chauviniste view on Derrida

indicators.note: only some of the phrase is used, so the answer is a part of it

parts.note: chauviniSTE VIEW ON DERrida

explanation.surface: A critic sniffs at a French male-chauvinist take on the philosopher Derrida.
explanation.walkthrough: The French spelling 'chauviniste' is chosen to supply the STE that starts the answer; an English 'chauvinist' would not have it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevie Wonder is a recording artist, the singer-songwriter behind Superstition.

clue.text: Peninsula south of sierra where it can get pretty cold

definitions.text: where it can get pretty cold

indicators.note: in a down answer, a piece south of another is written below it

parts.note: Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Iberian peninsula: Spain and Portugal

explanation.surface: A geography note: a peninsula lying south of a mountain range, where the weather turns chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sierra' looks like a mountain range next to a peninsula, but it is only the letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: Siberia is famous for its bitterly cold winters.

clue.text: Inspire love for Romanesque works without title

indicators.note: what remains works, as in ferments or is worked into shape, so its letters are rearranged
the word Romanesque is left without the letters of the title, so they are removed from it

parts.note: Esq. (esquire) is a title written after a man's name

explanation.surface: Romanesque architecture, untitled, inspires affection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes ESQ (esquire) from ROMANESQUE, leaving ROMANUE; 'works' then rearranges those seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour someone is to fill them with love or fascination, the same as inspiring love for them.

clue.text: Gauche, popular character such as Nellie leaves pub for good

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: the pub abbreviation leaves the character's name, coming out of it
the good abbreviation goes in to stand for the letters that left

parts.note: Nellie the Elephant is the elephant of a well-known British children's song
PH is the map abbreviation for public house

explanation.surface: An awkward, beloved figure like Nellie walks out of a pub for good.
explanation.walkthrough: Nellie the Elephant is a 1950s British children's song. 'for good' reads as a swap: the pub's letters leave and the good letter stands for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Gauche describes someone socially awkward and lacking grace, which is what inelegant means.

clue.text: Game with husband starts to interrupt Sunday tea

indicators.note: take the starting letters of the next words

parts.note: w/ is the short form of with
h = husband
first letters of Interrupt and Sunday
tea is often spelt 'T' or 'char'; here T

explanation.surface: A husband joins a card game that keeps breaking into Sunday tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Every small word earns a letter here, even 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Whist is a trick-taking card game.

clue.text: Rather colourless, tight at the back, tailored Lauren trousers

indicators.note: used as a verb: the rearranged name trousers, pockets, the last letter of tight
Lauren's letters are tailored, cut and restyled into a new order
only the letter at the back of tight is used

parts.note: its last letter is T

explanation.surface: A fashion note: Ralph Lauren's tailored trousers are fairly drab and snug at the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' is a verb here: the tailored name pockets the last letter of tight, splitting NEURAL after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A neutral shade is a muted beige or grey, a colour with little colour in it.

clue.text: Molière, who never pens a novel

indicators.note: the words enclose the answer, as a pen holds animals

parts.note: MolièRE, WHO Never

explanation.surface: A teasing claim that the French playwright Molière never wrote a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like 'writes', suiting a playwright, but it means 'encloses'. Erewhon is Samuel Butler's 1872 satire; the title is 'nowhere' spelt nearly backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Samuel Butler's 1872 satire of a topsy-turvy utopia.

clue.text: First appearance of Sidney Poitier, nuts about bogus religion

indicators.note: the letters are turned about into a new order
take the first letter of Sidney

parts.note: first letter of Sidney
part of the fodder
part of the fodder, not the indicator

explanation.surface: The actor Sidney Poitier's debut, when he was crazy about a sham faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' is the obvious anagram signal, but its letters are needed; 'about' does the stirring.
explanation.definitionFit: Superstition is irrational belief, a kind of false or bogus religion.

clue.text: Bank Holiday crossword: unlimited fury and resentment

indicators.note: the word loses its limits, its first and last letters

parts.note: British papers print an extra-large Jumbo crossword on bank holidays
JUMBO without its first and last letters
rage = fury

explanation.surface: The solver's rage and bitterness at a fiendish holiday puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: A bank holiday is a British public holiday; papers mark it with a bumper 'Jumbo' crossword. 'Unlimited' looks like it describes the fury but trims JUMBO.
explanation.definitionFit: To take umbrage is to feel resentment or offence.

clue.text: Routine fluttering within the womb?

indicators.note: the letters flutter into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A baby's regular kicking felt inside the womb.
explanation.walkthrough: The fluttering suits an unborn baby's movements, so the indicator belongs to the picture too.
explanation.definitionFit: In utero is Latin for 'in the womb'.

clue.text: The eleven-plus for one meant revising a set of books

parts.note: the eleven-plus is an exam once sat by English 11-year-olds for grammar school places, an example of an old test

indicators.note: meant is being revised, its letters reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Swotting for the eleven-plus exam meant going over a set of textbooks.
explanation.walkthrough: The eleven-plus was a British school-selection exam at age eleven, now largely abolished, hence an OLD TEST. 'revising' rearranges MEANT to AMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament is the first part of the Christian Bible, a collection of thirty-nine books.

clue.text: Each gown fitted with large area for hanging jewellery

parts.note: ea. = each

indicators.note: the gown has the large letter fitted inside it

parts.note: a robe is a gown; it takes in L after its R
L = large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Every dress comes with a large section for hanging jewellery on.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a fashion display where gowns are hung with jewels; the definition is the whole phrase after 'large'.
explanation.definitionFit: The earlobe is where earrings hang.

clue.text: Burnt toast or cheddar sandwiches

indicators.note: the words hold the answer between them like a sandwich filling

parts.note: toasT OR CHEDdar

explanation.surface: A menu of scorched toast or cheese sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' seems to be food on the menu; it is a verb meaning 'holds inside'.
explanation.definitionFit: Torched means set alight or burnt.

clue.text: Celeb boarding international flight

indicators.note: the star takes the international letter on board, inside it

parts.note: a celeb is a star
I = international; it goes inside STAR

explanation.surface: A celebrity getting on an international flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' is an aeroplane in the surface but a flight of steps in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stair, or flight of stairs, is a series of steps.

clue.text: Hair tint? No… he's bald, unfortunately

indicators.note: the letters end up in an unlucky new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a hair colour, then remembers the man has no hair to colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that ash-blonde is one example of a hair tint.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash-blonde is a pale, greyish blonde shade of hair colour.

clue.text: Instrument, according to Spooner, to damage old DDR leader

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two pieces exchange their first consonants

parts.note: to mar is to damage or spoil
Erich Honecker led East Germany (the DDR) until 1989; his name is said aloud

explanation.surface: An odd instruction attributed to Spooner: to harm the former East German leader.
explanation.walkthrough: MAR HONECKER, with its first sounds swapped as Spooner would, comes out as HAR MONICA.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonica is a mouth organ, a small wind instrument played by blowing and sucking through reeds.

clue.text: Examiner returned rubbish porcini to Northern Italy

indicators.note: the whole string is sent back, read right to left

parts.note: rot = nonsense, rubbish
cep is the French name for the porcini mushroom
N = northern
I is Italy's international vehicle code

explanation.surface: A food inspector sends a bad batch of porcini back to northern Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: ROT CEPS N I reversed gives INSPECTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspector is someone who examines things officially.

clue.text: South American spirit upset first-class fighter

parts.note: SA = South American

indicators.note: in a down answer, upset turns the word upside down, reading it backwards

parts.note: rum is a spirit
A1 = first-class, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: A South American drink knocked back upsets a champion boxer.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-rate; crosswords read the digit 1 as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the sword-carrying warrior class of feudal Japan.

clue.text: Our home base dad finally insulated

parts.note: Earth is the planet we live on
e is the base of natural logarithms

indicators.note: only the final letter of dad is used

parts.note: its last letter is D

explanation.surface: Dad has insulated the family's home base.
explanation.walkthrough: In maths, e is the base of natural logarithms, a common crossword source of E. Earthed is the gardener's sense: soil heaped around plants to protect them.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants that are earthed up have soil banked round them to protect them from frost, so they are insulated.

clue.text: Daughter knocked back drink in storehouse

parts.note: d = daughter

indicators.note: the drink is sent backwards, read right to left

parts.note: to tope is to drink heavily

explanation.surface: A daughter downs a drink inside a warehouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' is a drinker's phrase for swallowing, which suits the surface, and it also reverses TOPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is a place where goods are stored.

clue.text: Failed student doctor on strike stuck with operation

indicators.note: the operation is stuck in between the two other parts

parts.note: Dr = doctor
workers on strike are out
op = operation; it goes between DR and OUT

explanation.surface: A trainee medic who walked out on strike is stuck with an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical words all belong to one hospital scene, which hides that 'Failed student' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dropout is a student who leaves a course without finishing it.

clue.text: Woodward & Bernstein? They'll deliver!

definitions.meaning: the Washington Post reporters who broke Watergate
those who bring the mail to your door

explanation.surface: The Watergate reporters, promising they will deliver the story.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein were Post men in a newspaper sense; the question mark marks the playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Postmen deliver the mail; Woodward and Bernstein were men of the Washington Post.

clue.text: Son runs off, poaches English duck

parts.note: poaching and simmering are both gentle cooking
s = son; remove it to leave IMMERS
E = English

explanation.surface: A boy flees the kitchen after stealing and cooking an English duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poaches' and 'duck' make a cookery or game-hunting scene; duck is the verb, to dip under water.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck something is to plunge it under water, to immerse it.

clue.text: Brainy Swiss the French detained in their street heading north

indicators.note: the French article is held inside the street
in a down answer, the street is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: rue is French for street; turned round it is EUR, split EU…R
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A clever Swiss visitor held up by the French in one of their streets going north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Their' points back to the French, so the street is a French one.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhard Euler was a brilliant Swiss mathematician.

clue.text: American pouched very large amount after work

definitions.note: adjective phrase standing for the animal: the American pouched one

indicators.note: the other pieces come after the work

parts.note: op. = opus, a work
OS = outsize
a sum is an amount

explanation.surface: An American pocketed a huge sum after doing a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pouched' seems to mean pocketed, but it describes the animal: the opossum carries its young in a pouch.
explanation.definitionFit: The opossum is America's native marsupial, a pouched mammal.

clue.text: Wife ran around chased by Prince Harry, the horny beast

indicators.note: chased by means followed by, so the prince comes after
around means turned round, so wife and ran are written backwards

parts.note: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's name for the young Henry V, Harry

explanation.surface: A wife running away from a lustful Prince Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Harry suggests the modern royal, but here it is Shakespeare's Prince Hal; the horn is the narwhal's long tusk.
explanation.definitionFit: The narwhal is an Arctic whale whose male has a long spiral tusk, so a creature with a horn.

clue.text: Comic character of golf club member's first article

parts.note: an iron is a type of golf club

indicators.note: take the first letter of member

parts.note: first letter of member
an = indefinite article

explanation.surface: A club newsletter's opening piece about a funny golf-club member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golf club' reads as the club you join, beside 'member', but it is the stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron Man is a Marvel comic-book superhero.

clue.text: Rent Grade I building in outskirts of Kingston where there's little development

indicators.note: the rebuilt letters sit in between the outskirts
only the outer letters of Kingston, its first and last, are used

parts.note: its outer letters are K and N

indicators.note: the letters of the words are being built into a new structure

explanation.surface: A grand Grade I listed building in Kingston is to be rented out, a property listing.
explanation.walkthrough: Grade I is the top category of protected historic building in England. 'building' rearranges RENTGRADEI, which goes 'in' the outskirts K and N.
explanation.definitionFit: A kindergarten is a nursery school, where small children develop, a playful reading of little development.
